nameStory: The 'small-leaved lime' name comes from its distinctively petite, heart-shaped leaves that are notably smaller than its relatives. Don't let the 'lime' part fool you though - this tree has nothing to do with citrus fruits! The name comes from the Old English 'lind,' meaning flexible or pliant, referring to the tree's famously soft, workable wood that carvers have prized for centuries.
description: Small-leaved lime is a graceful deciduous tree that typically grows 50-80 feet tall with a rounded, dense crown. It's actually a European native that's been planted throughout New England as an ornamental street and park tree. The tree has a distinctive pyramidal shape when young, developing into a more rounded canopy with age, and produces clusters of small, fragrant yellowish flowers that dangle beneath heart-shaped leaves in early summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves about 2-3 inches long with finely serrated edges and a distinctly asymmetrical base - one side of the heart is slightly larger than the other. Feel the underside for tiny tufts of rusty-brown hairs tucked into the vein angles.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of 5-7 small, creamy-yellow flowers hang from a papery, wing-like bract in early summer. The flowers have an intensely sweet, honey-like fragrance that can be detected from quite a distance on warm evenings.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark when young, developing shallow furrows and ridges with age. The bark has a slightly corky texture and remains relatively smooth compared to many other large trees.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round, fuzzy nutlets about the size of a pea that hang from the same papery wing-bract as the flowers. The nuts feel slightly ribbed when rolled between your fingers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, rounded crown with branches that often droop slightly at the tips, giving the tree a graceful, weeping appearance. Young trees have a neat pyramidal shape that's popular for landscaping.

habitat: In New England, you'll find small-leaved lime primarily as a planted ornamental tree in urban parks, along city streets, and in suburban landscapes. It thrives in well-drained soils and tolerates urban pollution better than many native trees, which is why it's popular with city planners. Look for it in downtown areas and established neighborhoods rather than wild forests.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late spring, and you can spot the characteristic heart shape and asymmetrical base as they unfurl. The smooth gray bark becomes more apparent as other trees leaf out.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the intensely fragrant flowers bloom in early summer, followed by the small hanging nutlets. The full canopy shows off the tree's distinctive rounded, dense crown.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn a clear yellow color before dropping, and the small nutlets may still be hanging from their papery bracts. The tree's branching pattern becomes more visible.
seasonality.winter: Identify by the smooth gray bark, rounded crown silhouette, and small pointed buds arranged alternately on the twigs. Some papery bracts may persist on branches.

funFact: The flowers of small-leaved lime are so beloved by bees that a single mature tree can produce enough nectar to make 40 pounds of honey in one season - and lime honey is considered a delicacy in Europe, prized for its unique minty flavor!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with American basswood, but small-leaved lime has much smaller leaves (2-3 inches vs 4-6 inches) and those telltale rusty hair tufts on the leaf undersides. Memory trick: 'Small-leaved lime has small leaves with small rusty tufts.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'lime tree,' this species is completely unrelated to citrus limes and belongs to the mallow family (same as hibiscus and cotton). In Europe, these trees are often called 'linden trees,' and you might see that name used interchangeably in New England, especially on plant tags and in landscaping catalogs.
compareHints: Small-leaved lime differs from American basswood by its much smaller leaves and the presence of rusty hair tufts on leaf undersides, while basswood has larger leaves that are completely smooth underneath. Silver lime, another planted relative, has leaves that are distinctly silvery-white on the undersides, making it easy to distinguish when the wind flips the foliage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American basswood is the only native Tilia species in New England, making it unique in its genus here.

Silver lime differs from our native American basswood by its smaller, more densely fuzzy leaves with bright silvery undersides, while basswood has larger leaves that are only lightly hairy and pale green beneath.
